title: Isaac thought he was choosing a son.
paragraphs: Isaac thought he was choosing a son.
But he was actually shaping generations.
And one quiet sentence buried in Scripture reveals a tragedy most people skip past too quickly:
“Now Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob.” — Genesis 25:28
Read that again.
Isaac loved Esau because of what Esau gave him.

Not because Esau walked with God.
Not because Esau valued spiritual things.
Not because Esau carried the heart of the covenant.
Isaac loved him because Esau satisfied his appetite.
And that one misplaced affection changed everything.

Most people don’t realize how dangerous favoritism becomes when it blinds spiritual discernment. Isaac was not just a father. He was the patriarch chosen in the covenant line of Abraham. The promises of God were flowing through his household. Nations were in the womb of Rebekah. Heaven itself had already spoken concerning the boys before they were born:
“The elder shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23
God already declared Jacob would carry the covenant promise.
But Isaac kept leaning toward Esau anyway.
Why?
Because Esau appealed to his flesh.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can love someone emotionally and still be blind spiritually.

Isaac saw Esau’s strength.
His masculinity.
His hunting skills.
His outdoorsman spirit.
The wild game he brought home.
But God saw deeper.
God saw a man who would eventually despise his birthright for a bowl of stew.
A man willing to trade eternal inheritance for temporary hunger.
“And Esau despised his birthright.” — Genesis 25:34
That line should terrify people.
Because many still do the same thing today.

Trading purity for pleasure.
Truth for popularity.
Calling for comfort.
Conviction for temporary satisfaction.
God saw it.
You knew.

Esau was impulsive.
Driven by appetite.
Controlled by the immediate.

And Isaac either ignored it…
or refused to confront it.

That is one of the most painful realities in Scripture:
parents can sometimes strengthen what God is trying to expose.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The house of Isaac slowly became divided by favoritism.

Rebekah clung to Jacob.
Isaac clung to Esau.
And eventually deception entered the home because spiritual leadership had already weakened long before Jacob stole the blessing.
People often focus only on Jacob’s deception. And yes, Jacob sinned. Deeply.
But the fracture started earlier.
It started when affection became partial instead of righteous.

Isaac knew the prophecy.
Isaac knew God’s word concerning the boys.
Yet in Genesis 27, when Isaac became old and his eyes were dim, he still attempted to give the covenant blessing to Esau privately.
That matters.

His physical blindness mirrored something deeper:
spiritual blindness.
“And Isaac said unto Esau… make me savory meat, such as I love… that my soul may bless thee before I die.” — Genesis 27:4

Again…
his appetite appears.
The blessing moment was surrounded by craving.
That should shake people.
Because unchecked flesh can distort judgment even in spiritual leaders.

You can preach.
Lead.
Teach.
Raise children.
Carry history with God…
…and still allow personal desires to cloud obedience.
This story is not just about ancient brothers.
It is about what happens when families stop seeing through God’s eyes.

One child becomes “the successful one.”
Another becomes “the difficult one.”
One receives affection more freely.
Another grows up starving for approval.
And slowly division grows in silence.
Some people reading this still carry wounds from partial love.

You remember trying harder.
Performing better.
Hoping someone would finally choose you.
God saw it.
But this story is also a warning to parents.

Love cannot be governed by preference.
It must be governed by truth.

Isaac preferred Esau’s personality.
God chose according to purpose.
That difference changed history.
Romans 9 later explains that God’s choice was never based merely on human effort or natural status:
“For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil… it was said unto her, The elder shall serve the younger.” — Romans 9:11-12
This was about God’s sovereign plan.
Not human favoritism.

Not charisma.
Not talent.
Not natural strength.
Because the Kingdom of God has always overturned human expectations.

David was overlooked.
Joseph was hated.
Moses stuttered.
Peter failed.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God chose them.
Meanwhile Esau looked powerful externally…
…but spiritually he was careless.
Hebrews gives one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament about him:
“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” — Hebrews 12:16
Profane.
Meaning he treated holy things casually.
That spirit still exists everywhere now.

People casually ignore conviction.
Casually compromise.
Casually mock repentance.
Casually trade eternity for temporary pleasure.

One relationship.
One addiction.
One hidden sin.
One appetite.
And suddenly eternal things no longer matter.
That is Esau’s spirit.
And Isaac could not fully see it because his affections were clouded.
This is why spiritual discernment matters more than emotional attachment.

A person can be charming and still spiritually dangerous.
Talented and still rebellious.
Successful and still lost.

The flesh notices appearance first.
God examines the heart.
“For the Lord seeth not as man seeth… man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.” — 1 Samuel 16:7
But here is where the Gospel enters the story.
Because if we are honest…
there is Esau in all of us.
Every person has traded eternal things for temporary desires.
Every person has chosen appetite over obedience at some point.

Sin is not merely “mistakes.”
It is rebellion against God.

And the terrifying reality is this:
without Christ, we naturally drift toward Esau’s path.

Living for the now.
Living for self.
Living for appetite.
But Jesus came to rescue people enslaved to the flesh.
Where Esau failed, Christ obeyed.

Esau surrendered inheritance for food.
Jesus refused Satan’s temptation in the wilderness despite extreme hunger.
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4
Do you see the contrast?

Esau said yes to appetite.
Jesus said yes to the Father.
That obedience led Christ to the cross.
There, Jesus bore the punishment for sinners who traded holiness for sin again and again.
The cross is where mercy met rebels.

Not because we deserved it.
Not because we performed well enough.
But because God loved sinners enough to send His Son.
And through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, even people who wasted years chasing temporary things can be redeemed.
That is the hope Esau never truly sought.
Some of you feel the Holy Spirit exposing things right now.

The appetite.
The compromise.
The hidden idol.
The resentment.
The favoritism.
The spiritual blindness.
Do not harden your heart.
Because eventually repeated compromise numbs conviction.
That is why Scripture says:
“Today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.” — Hebrews 3:15
Today.
Not later.
Some people keep waiting for a “better season” to surrender to God while feeding the very desires destroying them.
You already know the emptiness isn’t leaving.
You knew.
But Jesus Christ still saves.

Still restores.
Still forgives.
Still changes hearts.

Because one path feeds the flesh until eternity is lost.
The other leads to Christ, repentance, and life.
